newsitem.title: JAPAN: Post-Deng era to bring little comfort to N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: Post-Deng era to bring little comfort to N.Korea.

text.p: The death of Deng Xiaoping is a symbolic loss to North Korea's old-style communist leaders, cutting a key link to their past and perhaps even helping moderates in their tottering system, analysts said on Thursday.

The passing of China's paramount leader was the second dose of bad news for North Korea in a week from Beijing, where the most senior official ever to defect from Pyongyang has been holed up in South Korea's embassy awaiting clearance to settle in Seoul.

Beijing has trodden a fine line between traditional ally North Korea and new business partner South Korea in handling defector Hwang Jang-yop, but Pyongyang cannot count on Chinese forbearance in the post-Deng era, analysts said.

"The death of Deng Xiaoping is bad news for North Korea, which had strong relations with China, particularly with senior Chinese military officials and bureaucrats who attached great importance to relations between the two countries," said Terumasa Nakanishi, professor of international politics at Kyoto University.

China and North Korea fought side by side against the United States and South Korea in the 1950-53 Korean War and as militant communist states with a long shared border they enjoyed a relationship they termed "as close as lips and teeth".

But the pragmatic market economic policies China adopted under Deng in the 1980s diverged from the hard-line statist policies of Pyongyang, which irritated Beijing by boasting of self-sufficiency while depending on Chinese handouts and goods at cheap "friendship" prices.

Politically, as a standard-bearer for world communism, China was embarrassed by North Korean cult worship of state founder Kim Il-sung and by the planned dynastic succession to his son Kim Jong-il, Pyongyang's de facto leader.

If the death of the Chinese-speaking Kim Il-sung in July 1994 shook the foundation of bilateral ties, Deng's passing could see relations grow even more fragile, said Nozomu Akizuki, professor of northeast Asian diplomacy at Tokyo's Meiji Gakuin University.
"Relations between China and North Korea were held together by a feeling of solidarity between old revolutionaries. Deng was about the last of those revolutionaries," he said.

Beijing's new rulers, imbued with Dengist economic pragmatism, are likely to snub North Korea, an erratic, impoverished state that reminds Chinese of their bitter past, in favour of South Korea, which dazzles with the promise of a prosperous future, analysts said.

"Chinese President Jiang Zemin, who decided to establish diplomatic relations with South Korea, apparently does not like North Korea very much," said Noriyuki Suzuki, a North Korea analyst at Tokyo-based Radiopress news service.
"But that does not necessarily mean that China will stop giving assistance to North Korea," he added.

Many observers say Beijing dreads the outright collapse of North Korea for the chaos and the tide of refugees it would unleash along China's borders, and especially for the loss of Chinese influence on the Korean peninsula.

To preserve its influence, China is likely to back Pyongyang's reformers, represented by defectors like Hwang, against military hard-liners as the best hope of keeping North Korea intact, said Katsumi Sato, director of the Modern Korea Institute.

"China supports the status quo, and fears that a hard-line military government would be inept at governing the country and resort to war," he said. "A war against South Korea would be won by the South and the United States, removing Chinese influence," Sato told reporters.
